1: This is Book 09's SD-WAN design on Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN, an implementation guide from the research section of the Federal Modernization Workbook, still under review.
Book 09 sets a vendor-neutral design for governed branch transport, and its field-office chapter already uses Catalyst edges as its costable example.
So this guide builds on the program's platform, consolidating rather than adding another vendor.
It's an example, not an endorsement by any agency.

In about fifteen minutes we'll cover the emergency directive that gates the build, the hosted-or-on-premises decision, the twelve-hub fabric, hardening, the TIC and Microsoft 365 paths, and the evidence the fabric has to emit.
First, why start with a directive?
2: Most build plans start with hardware.
This one starts with a directive, because the product we're building on was the subject of a 2026 emergency directive.
Book 09 already says the governor has its own exposure: one control plane with authority over every edge, and an internet-facing edge in every office.
On Catalyst SD-WAN that isn't hypothetical.
sis-uh's catalog now lists nine exploited flaws in the platform, and every 2026 advisory names Cisco's hosted fed-ramp environment among the affected deployments.
So the first gate is proving the control plane is patched, hunted and hardened, before it carries a single production flow.
3: Emergency Directive 26-03 landed on February 25, 2026, and it was strict about order: identify every Manager and Controller, collect logs and forensic images, update to Cisco's fixed releases, hunt, harden, and report.
The inventory was due to sis-uh the next night, and the fixed releases by five PM on February 27.
A March update added log delivery to CLAW, sis-uh's log warehouse, and a fourth report.
Those deadlines are past, and whether a new fabric must report is a question for sis-uh.
The program's position is simpler: a new build runs the same sequence anyway, because it's the best published definition of a clean control plane.
And the list of flaws kept growing.
4: The directive started with two catalog entries.
Today sis-uh's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog lists nine for Catalyst SD-WAN.
Six carry the directive's mitigation instructions, and three more arrived in June and September.
Two are authentication bypasses that reach the Manager, the Controller and the Validator.
The newest, added on September 30, came with a three-day due date.
So this isn't a one-time cleanup.
Nine exploited flaws in eight months is a patch tempo, not an event; treat the catalog as a standing posture.
Cisco now publishes advisories on the first and third Wednesday of each month, with a week's notice, and still goes out of cycle for active exploitation.
So which release do you need?
5: Reading Cisco's advisories together gives a floor: a minimum release per software train, one for the Manager and one for the Controller and Validator.
That's the program's inference from Cisco's tables, so re-read them at build time.
Several older trains have no fix of their own, and Cisco's answer is to migrate.
The newest train isn't listed for the Controller and Validator in three advisories, so ask Cisco.
And the edges have their own catalog entries, for the web interface and SNMP, so the HTTP server stays off and SNMPv3 sits behind an access list.
Cisco's Live Protect shields can bridge a gap, but Cisco calls them temporary partial protection.
6: Patching doesn't tell you whether someone already came through, and sis-uh's supplemental guidance is sobering.
The original bypass was exploited as a zero-day, the attacker's rogue device looked like a legitimate SD-WAN component, and the activity likely began in 2023, so the hunt reaches back that far.
The six-part hunt looks for downgrades and reboots, rogue peering, SSH key abuse, root sign-ins and cleared logs, and any root compromise means rebuilding from patched images.
The hardening is concrete: five-minute timeouts, pairwise IPsec keys, an enterprise certificate on the Manager, and sim alerts on unexpected peering.
The fabric carries no production traffic until every line of the gate is closed and evidenced.
7: First, decide where the control plane lives.
Cisco's fed-ramp environment, Catalyst SD-WAN for Government, is certified at Moderate, runs in AWS GovCloud, and is run by a Cisco federal operations team.
The guide recommends it by default.
sis-uh's own hardening guidance points there, Cisco patches the control plane, the boundary question gets an inherited, certified answer, and a fourteen-VM build goes away.
Choose on-premises if the system is High or isolated, if the authorizing official needs custody of forensic images, or if Cisco can't commit to the catalog's due dates.
But hosting doesn't remove the gate.
The hosted environment was affected too, and the edges, logs, allow-lists, roles and single sign-on stay the agency's.
8: Here's Book 09's target: two data centers, ten regional hubs, and about fifteen hundred field offices on an overlay.
On Catalyst, that's one edge per office, a high-availability pair at each hub, and hub-and-spoke to a regional hub, with a second hub as fallback.
In plain terms, the Manager is where you configure and monitor, the Validator decides which edges get in, and the Controller hands every edge its routes and policy.
On-premises, Cisco's sizing for this fleet is seven VMs per data center, fourteen in all, which matches Book 09's bill of materials.
The Manager cluster tops out at two thousand devices, so this fleet uses about three quarters of it.
9: Book 09 splits branch traffic into two classes.
Lean is the latency-sensitive kind: sign-in, voice, clock sync and interactive work.
Bulk is backups, patch waves and re-syncs.
On Catalyst, both become application-aware routing.
Lean gets a custom SLA class built from the pilot's measurements, not Cisco's defaults; it prefers the internet circuit and can fall back to 5G.
Bulk stays on the internet circuit, kept off 5G by data policy and behind lean traffic by QoS.
Every path that can reach the internet lands on the same security policy, so no path gets less rigor.
And lane discipline carries over unchanged: the program observes and emits evidence, while the Manager and Controllers route and enforce.
10: Transport and management each get their own VPN, with management out of band.
Then each admission segment becomes a service VPN.
Production reaches the hubs and the security service.
Remediation reaches only update and antivirus endpoints.
IoT and OT reach only their own management systems.
And guests go out through the security service, with no route inward.
Cisco ISE plugs in two ways: security group tags on the edge, or identity-based firewall rules.
One catch to remember: Cisco says TrustSec isn't supported with FIPS mode on.
So if the edges must run FIPS, segment by VPN and leave tag enforcement to the access switches.
11: Out of the box, Catalyst trusts Cisco's own P K I, and hardware edges prove who they are with a certificate in their trust chip.
An edge joins only if its serial number is on the authorized list.
Book 09 wants edges onboarded with certificates from the agency's P K I, and Cisco's Enterprise Certificate option makes that possible on recent IOS XE releases.
It's automatic at onboarding, but Cisco says later renewals need manual intervention.

So this is a build plus a procedure, not a setting: issue through the CLM platform, inventory certificates from the Manager's API, and write renewal as a runbook triggered by the Manager's expiry alarm.
The CyberArk certificate guide covers that platform.
12: If an acquisition has to state a FIPS 140-3 expectation, the honest answer has two halves.
The control components are in good shape: FIPS mode is on by default on recent releases and in the hosted environment, and Cisco's letter for the current train cites an active FIPS 140-3 module.
Their crypto modules are validated, but Cisco's current letters don't name SD-WAN mode, NIAP's router listings don't mention it, and Cisco's own example shows an edge with FIPS mode disabled.
So get edge validation in SD-WAN mode as a written vendor commitment before award.
There's no SD-WAN STIG either; the router STIGs are a reference baseline, not a checklist.
13: Book 09 names four branch egress patterns, and each has a Catalyst build.
Pattern A, the hairpin, sends internet traffic to the regional hub, which breaks out through its own security tunnel.
That's every office's starting state, and its fallback.
Pattern B, bare local breakout, is never allowed, so audit the policy group for it on every change.
Pattern C, the reference, is automatic IPsec tunnels from each edge to a security service edge, with Microsoft 365 Optimize traffic going direct only under its exception.
Pattern D puts policy in the endpoint agent, and the edge keeps agentless devices on A or C. Cisco's own TIC guide predates the current use case, so build to Book 09's reading.
14: For the security service, Cisco's government option is Secure Access for Government, certified at High, with automatic tunnels documented from a Catalyst branch.
But it runs in one region, Virginia, and a western office pays that round trip.
Measure it in the pilot, or choose a service with nearer points of presence.

Microsoft's Global Secure Access is available in G C C, and Catalyst is a listed partner, but Cisco's guide forwards only the Microsoft 365 profile, and Conditional Access applies only to users running the client.
So it carries branch Microsoft 365 traffic, not a full Pattern C.
And in G C C, informed network routing is still closed, so Microsoft 365 path choice rests on the edge's own probes.
15: Book 09 expects decision records that become boundary-change evidence.
On Catalyst, they're derived from the Manager's APIs, and labeled as derived.
Device inventory, the audit log, alarms and path statistics give you the controller, the selected path, the SLA state, failovers and the policy references.
Logs leave the box over TLS syslog to the sim, and all SD-WAN syslog goes to sis-uh through CLAW.
The documented connector's syslog path, through the Azure Monitor Agent, is fine.
Its NetFlow path uses an API whose support ended in September.
Ingestion continues, but treat that path as legacy.
Next, how the build is sequenced.
16: The build follows Book 09's own sequence, and each step leaves evidence.
Step zero is the gate we've covered.
Phase zero, the first six months, decides hosted or on-premises, sets the release baseline, runs a ten-site pilot, and starts the CLAW coordination and the static-address plan.
Phase one builds the twelve hubs, with SLA classes set from the pilot's measurements, and no office gets local internet until its security tunnel is up and its boundary change is approved.
Phase two moves offices in waves at MPLS renewal, retiring MPLS only after that office's logs reach CLAW.
Phase three adds the Microsoft 365 direct path and tracks the five retirement gates.
17: Three findings update Book 09's planning inputs.
First, sis-uh expects a static address on every edge.
That conflicts with zero-touch provisioning from dynamic addresses, and probably with the 5G secondary path.
It reinforces Book 09's deterministic-egress action, and it belongs in the circuit order.
Second, Book 09's cost model assumes an on-premises control plane, while sis-uh's guidance points to GovCloud.
Hosting replaces the fourteen-VM line with a subscription the model doesn't price yet.
Third, the catalog keeps growing, with the Validator now in scope and a floor that moves with every addition.
And one planning number: about four hundred seventy-six more edges, and the fleet needs a second overlay.
18: The control plane collects new exploited flaws faster than most agencies can patch, and a compromise may predate the build.
The answers are the hosted fabric with a written patch commitment, or a standing patch crew on Cisco's publication schedule, and hunting before you trust any existing fabric.

The medium risks are ones we've met: forensic custody on a hosted fabric, static addressing against zero-touch and 5G, a single-region security service, manual certificate renewal, and unconfirmed edge FIPS status.
The vendor asks turn those into questions with owners.
Cisco gets most of them; Microsoft, the carriers and sis-uh get one each.
19: The guide comes with a small example, a read-only Python script.
It checks every control component against the fixed releases for the directive and the catalog, and writes a gate file that must show no fail or confirm rows.
It exports a fleet inventory record per device, and an audit record per audit-log entry, flagging sign-ins and sources outside the management network.
It doesn't build path-decision records; those need the policy and statistics reads.
And it's read-only on purpose, because of lane discipline: the program observes, the fabric enforces.
Be clear about its status, though.
It's illustrative: unit-tested against mocked responses, not proven against a live fabric.
Finally, what to do with all of this.
20: To move this guide from under review to proved, build the gate and the ten-site pilot in a lab or a pilot fabric, run the example script against it, and record the evidence.
Some things couldn't be verified, like a Cisco recommended release and edge FIPS status in SD-WAN mode, so confirm those with Cisco.
The decisions are hosted or on-premises, the release baseline, static addressing, which security service, and the renewal runbook.
